title: When the Droop Divisor Divides the Voter Count, Droop Monroe Satisfies Droop-PJR+
abstract: In approval-based committee elections with $n$ voters and committee size $k$, the Droop Monroe rule assigns voters to committee candidates in groups of size $n/(k+1)$ to maximize the number of satisfied voters. When $k+1$ divides $n$, it is known that Droop Monroe satisfies Droop proportional justified representation (Droop-PJR), but whether it satisfies the stronger Droop-PJR+ axiom remained open in arXiv:2508.00811. We show that whenever $k+1$ divides $n$, every winning committee selected by the Droop Monroe rule satisfies Droop-PJR+. The proof proceeds by contradiction: if a cohesive voter group approving an unelected candidate were represented by fewer than $\ell$ committee members, the capacity bound on their assigned groups would leave more than $n/(k+1)$ unsatisfied voters jointly approving that candidate, contradicting an optimality lemma for Droop Monroe assignments. The theorem is formally verified in Lean.
introduction:
In approval-based committee elections, $n$ voters cast approval ballots over a set of candidates to select a committee of target size $k$. Proportional representation axioms evaluate whether sufficiently large groups of voters with cohesive preferences are guaranteed adequate representation in the winning committee. While classical axioms rely on the Hare quota $n/k$, recent work examines quotas based on the Droop quota $n/(k+1)$. The Hare Monroe rule assigns each selected committee member a group of approximately $n/k$ voters and maximizes the number of voters who approve their assigned candidate; the Droop Monroe rule operates analogously using groups of size $n/(k+1)$.

In "Justified Representation: From Hare to Droop" (arXiv:2508.00811), justified representation axioms are adapted to the Droop quota setting. A rule satisfies an axiom if every winning committee it selects satisfies the condition of the axiom. It is established in arXiv:2508.00811 that when $k + 1$ divides $n$, Droop Monroe satisfies Droop proportional justified representation (Droop-PJR) and Droop fully proportional justified representation (Droop-FPJR), whereas both axioms can be violated when $k + 1$ does not divide $n$.

The stronger axiom Droop-PJR+ strengthens Droop-PJR by considering groups of more than $\ell n / (k+1)$ voters who jointly approve at least one candidate outside the committee, requiring that such groups collectively approve at least $\ell$ committee members. Table 1 (note a) of arXiv:2508.00811 explicitly leaves open whether the Droop Monroe rule satisfies Droop-PJR+ when $k + 1$ divides $n$.

This post presents a formalized proof that when $k + 1$ divides $n$, every committee selected by the Droop Monroe rule satisfies Droop-PJR+, thereby answering the open question from arXiv:2508.00811.
result:
Let $n$ and $m$ be positive integers representing the number of voters and candidates, respectively, where each voter $i \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ has an approval set $A(i) \subseteq \{0, \dots, m-1\}$. Let $k$ be the target committee size, and assume that $k + 1$ divides $n$.

A committee $W \subseteq \{0, \dots, m-1\}$ of size $k$ satisfies Droop-PJR+ (`is_droop_pjr_plus`) if for every $\ell \in \{1, \dots, k\}$, every voter subset $S$ with $|S| > \ell n / (k + 1)$ that jointly approves a candidate outside $W$ (that is, there exists $c^* \notin W$ such that $c^* \in A(i)$ for all $i \in S$) satisfies
$$
\left| \left( \bigcup_{i \in S} A(i) \right) \cap W \right| \ge \ell.
$$
A committee $W$ is a Droop Monroe winning committee (`is_droop_monroe_committee`) if some Droop-valid assignment for $W$ scores at least as much as every Droop-valid assignment of every committee of size $k$.

The main result is `droop_monroe_satisfies_droop_pjr_plus`:

If $k + 1$ divides $n$, then every committee $W$ selected by the Droop Monroe rule satisfies Droop-PJR+.

In Lean, `droop_monroe_satisfies_droop_pjr_plus` quantifies over the voter and candidate counts $n, m : \mathbb{N}$, an approval profile $A : \mathrm{Fin}\;n \to \mathrm{Finset}\;(\mathrm{Fin}\;m)$, a committee size $k : \mathbb{N}$, and a committee $W : \mathrm{Finset}\;(\mathrm{Fin}\;m)$, asserting that if $(k + 1) \mid n$ and `is_droop_monroe_committee A k W` holds, then `is_droop_pjr_plus A k W` follows without restriction on the parameters.
proof:
Let $W$ be a committee selected by the Droop Monroe rule under approval profile $A$ with committee size $k$, assuming that $k+1$ divides $n$. By `is_droop_monroe_committee`, there exists an optimal Droop-valid assignment $\pi$ for $W$ that achieves the maximum score among all Droop-valid assignments of all committees of size $k$. Under $\pi$, each candidate in $W$ is assigned a group of at most $n/(k+1)$ voters, and an assigned voter is satisfied if and only if they approve their assigned candidate.

Suppose for contradiction that $W$ does not satisfy Droop-PJR+ (`is_droop_pjr_plus`). Then there exist an integer $\ell \in \{1, \dots, k\}$, a subset of voters $S$ with $|S| > \ell n / (k+1)$, and a candidate $c^* \notin W$ approved by all voters in $S$, such that the number of committee members approved by voters in $S$ is strictly less than $\ell$:
$$
|W_S| \le \ell - 1, \quad \text{where } W_S = \left(\bigcup_{i \in S} A(i)\right) \cap W.
$$

Consider which voters in $S$ can be satisfied under $\pi$. If a voter $i \in S$ is satisfied under $\pi$, they must be assigned to a candidate in $W$ whom they approve. By definition of $W_S$, any candidate in $W$ approved by any voter in $S$ must belong to $W_S$. Therefore, every satisfied voter in $S$ must be assigned by $\pi$ to a candidate in $W_S$.

Because $\pi$ is a Droop-valid assignment and $k+1$ divides $n$, each candidate in $W$ is assigned at most $n/(k+1)$ voters. Since $|W_S| \le \ell - 1$, the total number of voters in the entire election assigned to candidates in $W_S$ is at most
$$
|W_S| \cdot \frac{n}{k+1} \le (\ell - 1)\frac{n}{k+1}.
$$
Consequently, at most $(\ell - 1) n / (k+1)$ voters in $S$ can be satisfied by $\pi$.

Let $S_{\mathrm{unsat}}$ be the subset of voters in $S$ who are not satisfied under $\pi$. The size of $S_{\mathrm{unsat}}$ satisfies
$$
|S_{\mathrm{unsat}}| \ge |S| - (\ell - 1)\frac{n}{k+1} > \ell\frac{n}{k+1} - (\ell - 1)\frac{n}{k+1} = \frac{n}{k+1}.
$$
Thus, $S_{\mathrm{unsat}}$ contains strictly more than $n/(k+1)$ voters, all of whom are unsatisfied under $\pi$. Furthermore, because $S_{\mathrm{unsat}} \subseteq S$, every voter in $S_{\mathrm{unsat}}$ approves candidate $c^* \notin W$.

However, `droop_monroe_unsatisfied_group` (Lemma 2 of arXiv:2508.00811) states that if $k+1$ divides $n$ and $\pi$ is an optimal Droop-valid assignment for $W$, no group of more than $n/(k+1)$ voters who are all unsatisfied by $\pi$ can jointly approve a candidate outside $W$. This contradicts the existence of $S_{\mathrm{unsat}}$. It follows that $|W_S| \ge \ell$, which proves `droop_monroe_satisfies_droop_pjr_plus`.
discussion:
The theorem settles the open question posed in arXiv:2508.00811 (Table 1, note a) regarding whether Droop Monroe satisfies Droop-PJR+ when $k + 1$ divides $n$, answering it affirmatively.

This result specifically addresses the case where the Droop divisor $k + 1$ divides the number of voters $n$. When $k + 1$ does not divide $n$, Proposition 4 of arXiv:2508.00811 shows that Droop Monroe can violate Droop-PJR, which implies that Droop-PJR+ is also violated in that regime.

Furthermore, note a of Table 1 in arXiv:2508.00811 also groups Droop Greedy Monroe alongside Droop Monroe, noting that both rules satisfy Droop-PJR and Droop-FPJR when $k + 1$ divides $n$ (Theorem 4 of arXiv:2508.00811), while their status with respect to Droop-PJR+ was left open. The proof presented here relies directly on the global optimality of the assignment in the Droop Monroe rule via `droop_monroe_unsatisfied_group`, leaving the corresponding question for Droop Greedy Monroe open.
